prompt: What is Sprint Retrospective mainly for?
options: Planning ways to improve quality and effectiveness.
Prioritizing the Product Backlog.
Approving the Increment.
Reporting status to stakeholders.
explanation: The Retrospective is used to inspect how the Scrum Team worked and plan improvements.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Several Done Increments are created during one Sprint. Is that allowed?
options: No. Scrum allows exactly one Increment per Sprint.
Yes. Multiple Increments may be created, and they add to prior Increments.
Only if the Sprint is one month long.
Only when stakeholders approve each one.
explanation: Scrum allows multiple Increments during a Sprint. Each Done Increment builds on previous Increments and must remain usable.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Which Scrum value is most directly supported when people speak up about a problem that could threaten the Sprint Goal?
options: Focus
Courage
Respect
Commitment
explanation: It takes courage to raise difficult issues openly so the team can deal with reality rather than hide it.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A manager asks for individual Daily Scrum status reports. What is the best response?
options: Explain that the Daily Scrum is for Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal, not a management status meeting.
Agree, because Scrum requires individual status reporting.
Have the Product Owner collect the reports instead.
Cancel Daily Scrum and email the reports.
explanation: The Daily Scrum exists to help Developers inspect and adapt their plan, not to report upward.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: A team hides unfinished testing so Sprint Review looks successful. Which pillar of empiricism is most directly damaged?
options: Transparency
Inspection
Adaptation
Forecasting
explanation: If the true state of work is hidden, inspection and adaptation are based on bad information.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Several Scrum Teams work on one product. Do their Sprint schedules have to be identical?
options: Yes, Scrum requires all teams to start and end Sprints at the same moment.
No. Scrum does not require synchronized Sprint calendars, though teams still need to integrate their work effectively.
Only the Product Owner decides whether synchronization is legal.
Sprints may only be synchronized for software products.
explanation: Scrum does not require synchronized Sprint schedules across teams. What matters is effective coordination around one product and an integrated Done Increment.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Which two statements about velocity are consistent with Scrum?
options: Velocity can be a team's optional planning aid.
Velocity is a required Scrum commitment.
A higher velocity does not by itself prove that more value was created.
The Product Owner should set a velocity target for every Sprint.
explanation: Velocity may be useful as an optional local planning measure, but Scrum does not make it a commitment or a direct measure of value.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Which artifact has the Definition of Done as its commitment?
options: Product Backlog
Sprint Backlog
Increment
Product Goal
explanation: The Definition of Done is the commitment for the Increment.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Who is the Daily Scrum primarily for?
options: The Developers.
The Product Owner.
Stakeholders.
Management.
explanation: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Who has the authority to cancel a Sprint?
options: The Product Owner.
The Scrum Master.
The Developers.
Any stakeholder.
explanation: Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel a Sprint.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: A team collects lots of data but never changes course when the data shows a problem. Which part of empiricism is missing?
options: Adaptation.
Transparency.
Timeboxing.
Sizing.
explanation: Inspection only helps when the team is willing to adapt based on what it learns.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Which two signs suggest a Scrum Master is acting more like a traditional project coordinator than a Scrum Master?
options: Assigning tasks to individuals.
Coaching the team to solve its own workflow problem.
Collecting status from each Developer for management reporting.
Helping the Product Owner communicate a Product Goal.
explanation: Task assignment and individual status collection are command-and-control behaviors that work against Scrum's self-management.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: The team spends Sprint Review reading a long status deck and leaves no time for discussion. What is the main problem?
options: Sprint Review should be an inspection and adaptation working session, not just a presentation.
Sprint Review should only contain the Daily Scrum questions.
Stakeholders should not attend Sprint Review.
The Scrum Master must present instead.
explanation: Sprint Review works best as a collaborative working session focused on results, changed conditions, and next steps.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: True or False: The Definition of Done is a commitment associated with the Increment.
options: True
False
explanation: Scrum associates the Definition of Done with the Increment.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Which two are Developer accountabilities in Scrum?
options: Creating a plan for the Sprint.
Ordering the Product Backlog.
Adapting their plan each day toward the Sprint Goal.
Canceling the Sprint when scope changes.
explanation: Developers create the Sprint plan through the Sprint Backlog and adapt that plan as they learn.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Which two behaviors best demonstrate the Scrum value of Focus?
options: Keeping attention on the Sprint Goal during the Sprint.
Starting extra work whenever someone important asks.
Limiting distractions that do not help the current objective.
Avoiding stakeholder feedback until the project is finished.
explanation: Focus means concentrating on the work of the Sprint and the team's goals rather than constantly chasing unrelated work.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Why does Scrum favor smaller, cross-functional teams?
options: They tend to communicate better and can focus on creating value with fewer handoffs.
They guarantee higher velocity.
They eliminate the need for stakeholders.
They make the Product Owner unnecessary.
explanation: Smaller, cross-functional teams reduce coordination overhead and unnecessary dependencies.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: The Product Owner attends a Daily Scrum and starts directing individual work. What should the Scrum Master do?
options: Encourage it because the Product Owner owns all Scrum work.
Help everyone understand that the Daily Scrum is for Developers to inspect and adapt their plan.
Cancel the Sprint immediately.
Replace the Daily Scrum with written status reports.
explanation: The Daily Scrum is for Developers. Others may be present in some circumstances, but it should not become a command-and-control meeting.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: What should happen when inspection shows that the product or process has moved outside acceptable limits?
options: Adapt as soon as possible to reduce further deviation.
Wait until the next annual planning cycle.
Freeze the Product Backlog.
Increase the Sprint length.
explanation: Inspection without timely adaptation has little value. Scrum expects adjustment when important deviations are discovered.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Which response best supports self-management when Developers raise a workflow problem?
options: Help them understand the constraint and let them work out a solution where possible.
Immediately assign a process for them to follow.
Escalate every issue to management.
Have the Product Owner decide the team's workflow.
explanation: Scrum encourages self-managing teams. Coaching and removing impediments are better than unnecessary command-and-control.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: A manager wants to create separate testing and architecture sub-teams inside one Scrum Team. What should the Scrum Master explain?
options: That is required for teams larger than seven.
Scrum Teams do not contain sub-teams; accountability stays with the whole team and its accountabilities.
It is fine as long as the Product Owner approves.
Only the testing sub-team is allowed in Scrum.
explanation: Scrum Teams do not have sub-teams or internal hierarchies. Different skills can exist, but the team works as one unit.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A Scrum Master is asked to facilitate every Scrum event forever. What is the best long-term goal?
options: Remain the permanent meeting owner so Scrum stays consistent.
Help the Scrum Team become capable of running useful events without depending on the Scrum Master for every detail.
Move all events to email.
Have the Product Owner lead every event instead.
explanation: A Scrum Master may facilitate when useful, but coaching should increase the team's ability to use Scrum effectively without unnecessary dependency.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: For a one-month Sprint, what is the maximum timebox for Sprint Review?
options: Four hours.
Two hours.
Eight hours.
There is no timebox.
explanation: Sprint Review is timeboxed to a maximum of four hours for a one-month Sprint.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Which two ideas are central to Scrum theory?
options: Empiricism.
Lean thinking.
Critical path management.
Earned value control.
explanation: Scrum is founded on empiricism and lean thinking.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A company has a mandatory quality standard that applies to every product. How does that affect a Scrum Team's Definition of Done?
options: The team may ignore it if the Sprint Goal is urgent.
The team's Definition of Done must include at least that organizational standard.
The Scrum Master replaces it with a team-specific standard.
It only applies after release.
explanation: When an organizational Definition of Done or applicable standard exists, the Scrum Team must follow it as a minimum.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Which two statements about Sprint Review are correct?
options: It is a working session with stakeholders to inspect outcomes and discuss what to do next.
It is the formal approval gate for releasing the Increment.
The Product Backlog may be adapted based on what is learned.
Only the Product Owner may speak.
explanation: Sprint Review is a collaborative inspection of the Sprint's outcome with stakeholders, and what is learned may influence the Product Backlog.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A manager asks the Scrum Master to maintain a team burndown chart because 'Scrum requires one.' What should the Scrum Master say?
options: Correct; burndown charts are a required Scrum artifact.
Scrum does not require a burndown chart; the team may use one if it helps.
Only a burn-up chart is allowed.
Burndown charts are only allowed for one-week Sprints.
explanation: Scrum does not prescribe a specific progress-tracking chart. Teams may use useful techniques as long as they do not replace the framework's required elements.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: What makes up the Sprint Backlog?
options: The Sprint Goal, selected Product Backlog items, and the plan for delivering the Increment.
Only the Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint.
The Product Goal and every unfinished item from prior Sprints.
A list of tasks assigned by the Product Owner.
explanation: The Sprint Backlog contains the why, what, and how for the Sprint.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: True or False: Scrum Teams contain sub-teams such as testing, architecture, and analysis teams.
options: True
False
explanation: Scrum Teams are cross-functional and do not have sub-teams or hierarchies within the Scrum Team.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Which two statements about Scrum events are true?
options: They create regular opportunities for inspection and adaptation.
They mainly exist to provide management status reports.
Their timeboxes help create focus and reduce unnecessary meetings.
The Scrum Master must personally chair every event.
explanation: Scrum events provide a purposeful cadence for inspection and adaptation, and their timeboxes help keep that work focused.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Which artifact has the Sprint Goal as its commitment?
options: Product Backlog
Sprint Backlog
Increment
Release plan
explanation: The Sprint Goal is the commitment for the Sprint Backlog.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A Scrum Master notices the team is treating Scrum events like mandatory status meetings. What should the Scrum Master do first?
options: Cancel the events until the team is more mature.
Teach the purpose of the events and help the team make them useful.
Take over each event and run it personally.
Replace the events with weekly project reporting.
explanation: A Scrum Master helps everyone understand the purpose of Scrum events and works to keep them positive, productive, and within their timeboxes.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: True or False: Scrum requires each Developer to have a fixed job title and narrow specialty.
options: True
False
explanation: Scrum Teams are cross-functional. Individuals may have specialties, but the team collectively has the skills needed to create value.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: What is the Daily Scrum supposed to help the Developers do?
options: Inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adjust their plan.
Report status to the Product Owner.
Get task assignments from the Scrum Master.
Approve changes to the Product Backlog.
explanation: The Daily Scrum focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal and adaptation of the plan.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Which two responses fit the Scrum Master's approach to impediments?
options: Help the team cause important impediments to be removed.
Personally solve every impediment so the team never has to deal with them.
Coach the team so it becomes better at handling problems itself.
Put every impediment into the Product Backlog and wait.
explanation: The Scrum Master helps remove impediments while also strengthening the team's own ability to solve problems, rather than becoming a permanent dependency.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A Developer admits that an item will not meet the Definition of Done by Sprint end. Which Scrum value is being demonstrated most clearly?
options: Openness
Respect
Commitment
Focus
explanation: Openness includes being transparent about progress, problems, and what is actually Done.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A Developer asks the Scrum Master to decide which teammate should handle a difficult task. What is the best response?
options: Assign the most senior Developer.
Coach the Developers to decide how to organize the work themselves.
Ask the Product Owner to assign the task.
Delay the work until Retrospective.
explanation: The Scrum Master should support self-management rather than become a task allocator.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Which two signs would suggest the Developers are not really self-managing?
options: A manager assigns work to individuals.
Developers decide together how to organize the Sprint work.
The Product Owner tells each Developer exactly how to implement an item.
Developers adjust their plan as they learn.
explanation: Self-management means the team decides internally who does what, when, and how. Outside task assignment and implementation direction weaken that accountability.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A team has a person with deep testing expertise. Who is accountable for creating a quality Increment?
options: The Scrum Team as a whole, with Developers responsible for the work needed to create it.
Only the tester.
Only the Product Owner.
Only the Scrum Master.
explanation: Quality is not handed off to a separate Scrum accountability. The Scrum Team is accountable for a valuable, useful Increment.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: A Developer says, 'I finished my part, so the integration problem belongs to someone else.' Which Scrum idea does that conflict with most?
options: Shared accountability for creating a usable Increment.
Product Backlog ordering.
Sprint length.
Stakeholder management.
explanation: The Scrum Team is accountable for producing a valuable, useful Increment, not for maximizing isolated individual output.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: What must be true before work can count as part of the Increment?
options: It meets the Definition of Done.
The Product Owner has approved it.
It has been shown at Sprint Review.
It has been released to customers.
explanation: Work is part of the Increment only when it meets the Definition of Done.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Which statement about releasing a Done Increment is correct?
options: Release must wait for Sprint Review.
Release may happen whenever it makes sense; Sprint Review is not a release gate.
Only the Scrum Master may authorize a release.
A release may happen only once per Sprint.
explanation: A Done Increment can be delivered before the Sprint ends. Sprint Review is for inspection and adaptation, not release approval.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A distributed team keeps losing time because Daily Scrum logistics change every day. What would best reduce the overhead?
options: Use a consistent time and place or connection method.
Have the Scrum Master assign a different meeting room each day.
Replace the Daily Scrum with weekly status reports.
Invite management to coordinate the setup.
explanation: Scrum events are generally held at a consistent time and place to reduce complexity.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Which two things should the Scrum Team inspect during Sprint Retrospective?
options: How people interacted and worked together.
Whether the Product Owner's salary is competitive.
Processes, tools, and the Definition of Done when relevant.
Which stakeholders should receive individual performance scores.
explanation: Retrospective examines how the last Sprint went, including people, interactions, processes, tools, and quality practices.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A team finishes Sprint Planning in three hours during a one-month Sprint. Must it continue for the full eight hours?
options: Yes. The timebox is a required duration.
No. A timebox is a maximum; the event can end when its purpose has been achieved.
Only if the Scrum Master approves an early finish.
Only when the Product Owner leaves early.
explanation: A timebox is a maximum duration, not a required amount of time to consume.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: The Developers realize they selected too much work, but the Sprint Goal is still achievable. What should they do?
options: Work with the Product Owner to adjust scope while protecting the Sprint Goal.
Lower the Definition of Done for the Sprint.
Cancel the Sprint automatically.
Wait until Sprint Review to mention it.
explanation: Scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned, as long as the Sprint Goal is not endangered and quality does not decrease.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: A Scrum Master is working with executives who demand a fixed one-year scope. What is the most useful response?
options: Promise the scope because Scrum guarantees delivery dates.
Help them understand empirical planning and the value of adapting as more is learned.
Refuse to communicate with management because they are outside the Scrum Team.
Replace the Product Backlog with a Gantt chart.
explanation: The Scrum Master serves the organization by helping people understand empirical approaches to complex work and planning.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: True or False: A Done Increment may be released before the Sprint ends.
options: True
False
explanation: Scrum does not require waiting for Sprint Review or the end of the Sprint to release a Done Increment.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: During Sprint Planning, Developers break selected work into smaller work items. Who decides the decomposition?
options: The Developers
The Product Owner
The Scrum Master
The most senior architect
explanation: Developers decide how to decompose and organize the selected work.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A team keeps adding meetings to inspect the same work because the Scrum events are not useful. What is a better first move?
options: Make the existing Scrum events effective before adding more process.
Remove Sprint Review.
Turn the Daily Scrum into an hour-long status meeting.
Ask management to attend every event.
explanation: Scrum already provides a regular cadence for inspection and adaptation. If those events are weak, improving them is usually more useful than layering on more ceremony.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: True or False: Every Product Backlog item selected during Sprint Planning is a guarantee that it will be finished.
options: True
False
explanation: The selected work is a forecast. The Sprint Goal is the commitment.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: During Sprint Planning, who makes the call on how much work the Developers believe they can take on?
options: The Developers.
The Product Owner.
The Scrum Master.
The highest-ranking stakeholder.
explanation: Developers select the work they believe they can complete, informed by discussion with the Product Owner and by capacity, past performance, and the Definition of Done.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Who is accountable for creating a usable Increment each Sprint?
options: The Developers
The Product Owner
The Scrum Master
Stakeholders
explanation: Developers are accountable for creating a usable Increment each Sprint. The Scrum Team as a whole is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: For a one-month Sprint, what is the maximum timebox for Sprint Planning?
options: 2 hours
4 hours
8 hours
1 day plus the Daily Scrum
explanation: Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A Sprint ends Friday afternoon. When does the next Sprint begin?
options: Immediately after the previous Sprint concludes.
The following Monday.
After the Product Owner finishes refinement.
After a separate planning gap.
explanation: A new Sprint starts immediately after the conclusion of the previous Sprint.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: For a one-month Sprint, what is the maximum timebox for Sprint Retrospective?
options: Three hours.
Four hours.
Eight hours.
One full day.
explanation: Sprint Retrospective is timeboxed to a maximum of three hours for a one-month Sprint.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Which statement is true during a Sprint?
options: Quality does not decrease.
The Product Backlog cannot be refined.
The Sprint Backlog cannot change.
Stakeholders cannot provide feedback.
explanation: Scrum explicitly states that quality does not decrease during the Sprint.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Who owns and updates the Sprint Backlog?
options: The Developers.
The Product Owner.
The Scrum Master.
The project manager.
explanation: The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: True or False: The Sprint Review must be a formal demo presentation.
options: True
False
explanation: The Sprint Review is a working session. A demo can be useful, but Scrum does not require a formal presentation format.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: What are the three topics Sprint Planning addresses?
options: Why the Sprint is valuable, what can be done, and how the work will get done.
Who is on the team, who reports to whom, and who approves the release.
What failed last Sprint, who caused it, and how to prevent it.
Budget, staffing, and release approval.
explanation: Sprint Planning addresses why the Sprint is valuable, what can be done this Sprint, and how the chosen work will get done.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Which two statements are true about change during a Sprint?
options: Changes that endanger the Sprint Goal should be avoided.
No change of any kind is allowed once Sprint Planning ends.
Scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned.
The Scrum Master personally approves all scope changes.
explanation: A Sprint is not frozen. The team can learn and adjust scope with the Product Owner, but the Sprint Goal must remain protected.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Mid-Sprint, the Developers discover a better way to achieve the Sprint Goal. Can they update the Sprint Backlog?
options: Yes.
No.
explanation: The Sprint Backlog is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Who is accountable for effective Product Backlog management?
options: The Developers
The Product Owner
The Scrum Master
The project manager
explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for effective Product Backlog management, even when other people help with the work.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: True or False: A 'tester' on a Scrum Team has a separate Scrum accountability called Tester.
options: True
False
explanation: Scrum defines three accountabilities: Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers. Testing skills can exist within the Developers.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: A Developer wants to use a different Daily Scrum format from the usual three questions. Is that allowed?
options: No. Scrum requires the three-question format.
Yes. Developers may use any structure that helps them inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog.
Only if the Scrum Master writes the new format.
Only during the last week of a Sprint.
explanation: Scrum does not require a specific Daily Scrum script. Developers choose a structure that creates focus on the Sprint Goal and a useful plan for the next day.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A Sprint Goal is useful because it:
options: Gives the Sprint a single objective while allowing some flexibility in the exact work.
Guarantees every selected Product Backlog item will be finished.
Locks scope so nothing can change.
Replaces the Product Goal for the duration of the Sprint.
explanation: The Sprint Goal gives focus and coherence while allowing the plan to adapt as more is learned.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: What is the maximum timebox for the Daily Scrum?
options: 10 minutes
15 minutes
30 minutes
As long as needed
explanation: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: The Scrum Master is absent for a day. Can the Scrum Team still hold its Daily Scrum?
options: No. The Daily Scrum requires the Scrum Master.
Yes. The Daily Scrum is for Developers and does not depend on the Scrum Master's attendance.
Only if the Product Owner leads it.
Only if management approves.
explanation: The Daily Scrum belongs to the Developers. The Scrum Master helps them understand its purpose but does not need to attend or lead it.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: What is the purpose of timeboxes in Scrum?
options: To create a maximum amount of time for an event and encourage focus.
To guarantee the team finishes all planned work.
To give the Scrum Master authority over the team.
To prevent any discussion after the event ends.
explanation: Timeboxes set a maximum duration and help keep events focused without prescribing the exact minute-by-minute agenda.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A team asks why Scrum does not prescribe a specific estimation method. What is the best explanation?
options: Estimation is prohibited in Scrum.
Scrum defines a framework; teams may choose useful tactics that fit within it.
Only the Scrum Master is allowed to choose estimation methods.
All Product Backlog items must use hours instead.
explanation: Scrum defines the essential framework and leaves many context-specific techniques to the people using it.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A Scrum Team wants to skip Sprint Retrospective because the Sprint went well. What should the Scrum Master say?
options: That is fine when there were no defects.
Retrospective still happens each Sprint because improvement is ongoing.
Only the Product Owner decides whether Retrospective is needed.
Replace it with a longer Sprint Review.
explanation: The Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint and is used to plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness, even when things went well.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: True or False: A Sprint should be canceled whenever the Developers realize they cannot finish every selected Product Backlog item.
options: True
False
explanation: The selected work is a forecast. If the Sprint Goal is still useful, the team can adapt scope instead of canceling the Sprint.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: The Product Owner wants the Scrum Master to decide Product Backlog order during a disagreement. What should happen?
options: The Scrum Master should make the decision to stay neutral.
The Product Owner remains accountable for ordering the Product Backlog.
The Developers vote and the majority decides.
Stakeholders must reach unanimous agreement.
explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for effective Product Backlog management, including ordering. Others can advise, but the accountability remains with the Product Owner.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A team identifies a serious process problem in Retrospective. When should the improvement be addressed?
options: Only after the current release is finished.
As soon as practical; the team may even add it to the next Sprint Backlog if appropriate.
At the next annual planning meeting.
Only if management funds a separate improvement project.
explanation: Improvements are not meant to sit on a shelf. The team should address them as soon as practical, and important improvements may be added to the next Sprint Backlog.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A Sprint is three weeks long. What is the maximum length allowed by Scrum?
options: Two weeks
One month
Six weeks
There is no maximum
explanation: A Sprint is a fixed-length event of one month or less.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A Scrum Team keeps changing priorities every day and rarely finishes anything meaningful. Which Scrum value would most directly help correct this pattern?
options: Focus
Respect
Courage
Openness
explanation: Focus helps the team concentrate on a meaningful goal instead of constantly switching attention.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: True or False: Scrum can be used only for software development.
options: True
False
explanation: False. Scrum is used for complex work in many domains. The term Developers refers to the people doing the work needed to create value.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A senior engineer repeatedly dismisses a junior teammate's ideas without discussion. Which Scrum value is most obviously being ignored?
options: Respect
Focus
Commitment
Courage
explanation: Respect means treating people as capable professionals whose perspectives deserve consideration.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A Scrum Master sees the team solving a difficult problem on its own. What should the Scrum Master usually do?
options: Take over so the solution is correct.
Allow the team to self-manage and step in only when coaching or help is useful.
Escalate the problem immediately.
Assign a team lead to make the decision.
explanation: Scrum Masters support self-management. Solving every problem for the team can create dependence and weaken team capability.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: During Sprint Planning, the team needs technical advice from a specialist outside the Scrum Team. What is allowed?
options: No outsiders may ever be involved in Sprint Planning.
The Scrum Team may invite other people to provide advice.
The specialist must become the Scrum Master for that Sprint.
The specialist must approve the Sprint Goal.
explanation: The Scrum Team may invite other people to Sprint Planning to provide advice when that helps the planning work.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Why does Scrum use a Definition of Done instead of letting each person decide what 'finished' means?
options: To create a shared quality standard and make the state of the Increment transparent.
To let the Scrum Master grade Developers.
To eliminate the need for Product Backlog refinement.
To guarantee release dates.
explanation: The Definition of Done gives everyone a shared understanding of the quality measures required for work to count as part of the Increment.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: True or False: The Scrum Master is the team's manager and has final authority over how Developers do the work.
options: True
False
explanation: False. Developers are self-managing and decide how to turn selected Product Backlog items into a Done Increment.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: What does cross-functional mean for a Scrum Team?
options: Every person must be able to perform every skill equally well.
The team has the skills needed to create value each Sprint.
Each specialty must have its own sub-team.
The Scrum Master must fill any missing technical role.
explanation: Cross-functional means the team collectively has the skills needed to create value without relying on separate functional silos for normal delivery.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: True or False: Product Backlog refinement is a formal Scrum event with its own required timebox.
options: True
False
explanation: False. Refinement is an ongoing activity, not one of the formal Scrum events.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Who decides how Product Backlog items selected for a Sprint are turned into an Increment?
options: The Developers
The Product Owner
The Scrum Master
Stakeholders
explanation: How the work gets done is up to the Developers.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: How large should a Scrum Team typically be?
options: Exactly 7 people.
10 or fewer people in most cases.
At least 12 people so every specialty is represented.
Any size, as long as the Scrum Master approves it.
explanation: Scrum Teams are typically 10 or fewer people so they can stay nimble and communicate effectively.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A Scrum Master is helping a new Product Owner. Which two areas are appropriate to coach?
options: How to define a useful Product Goal.
How to assign daily tasks to Developers.
How to maintain an effective Product Backlog.
How to approve each Increment before it can be Done.
explanation: Scrum Masters help Product Owners with Product Goals and Product Backlog management, among other product-planning practices.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A manager asks what the Scrum Master is ultimately accountable for. What is the best answer?
options: Making sure every Developer stays busy.
The Scrum Team's effectiveness.
Approving the Product Backlog before Sprint Planning.
Assigning work so the Sprint finishes on time.
explanation: The Scrum Master is accountable for the Scrum Team's effectiveness and helps the team improve how it uses Scrum.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Which Scrum value is most visible when team members openly raise a risk instead of hiding it?
options: Openness.
Utilization.
Specialization.
Prediction.
explanation: Openness supports honest visibility into the work, problems, and risks.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: A team wants to lower its quality standard for one Sprint because it is behind. What is the best answer?
options: Do not lower quality simply to fit more scope into the Sprint.
Lower it if the Product Owner approves.
Lower it only for internal products.
Lower it if the Sprint Review is tomorrow.
explanation: Scrum states that quality does not decrease during a Sprint.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Which two statements fit Scrum?
options: It is a lightweight framework for complex work.
It prescribes the detailed engineering practices every team must use.
It leaves room for teams to add useful practices that fit within the framework.
It is a reporting method built around fixed scope.
explanation: Scrum provides a lightweight framework and intentionally leaves many context-specific practices to the people using it.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: If several Scrum Teams work on the same product, which set should they share?
options: Product Goal, Product Backlog, and Product Owner.
Sprint Goal, Sprint Backlog, and Daily Scrum.
Scrum Master, Sprint Backlog, and release calendar.
Only the Product Goal.
explanation: Teams working on one product share the Product Goal, Product Backlog, and Product Owner.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: The team discovers that an important assumption was wrong. What does empiricism suggest they should do?
options: Stick to the original plan so the metrics remain stable.
Adapt based on what they learned.
Wait until the release is complete before changing direction.
Ask management to rewrite the Scrum framework.
explanation: Empiricism depends on making work visible, inspecting what is happening, and adapting when new evidence shows a change is needed.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A team finishes coding a feature but has not completed testing required by its Definition of Done. How should the feature be treated?
options: It is not Done and should not be counted as part of the Increment.
It is Done because coding is complete.
It is Done if the Product Owner accepts the risk.
It becomes Done automatically at Sprint Review.
explanation: A Product Backlog item that does not meet the Definition of Done is not part of the Increment.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: True or False: Stakeholders are regular participants in the Sprint Retrospective.
options: True
False
explanation: The Sprint Retrospective is an event for the Scrum Team.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: A team wants a separate hardening Sprint after every three Sprints. What is the main Scrum concern?
options: Hardening Sprints must be exactly one week.
Work should meet the Definition of Done within the Sprint rather than relying on a later cleanup Sprint.
Only the Product Owner can perform hardening work.
Hardening is required only before major releases.
explanation: A Done Increment should satisfy the Definition of Done during the Sprint. Deferring required quality work to a later hardening Sprint hides the true state of the product.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Which two actions fit the Scrum Master's service to the Scrum Team?
options: Coaching the team in self-management.
Assigning specialists to Product Backlog items.
Helping remove impediments that slow the team's progress.
Writing the Sprint Backlog for the Developers.
explanation: The Scrum Master coaches self-management and helps the team cause impediments to be removed. The Developers own their Sprint Backlog and daily plan.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Why do Scrum artifacts have commitments?
options: To create transparency and focus around what each artifact represents.
To give managers a way to punish missed estimates.
To replace the need for inspection.
To make all scope fixed at the start of a project.
explanation: The commitments improve transparency and focus by clarifying the objective or quality standard tied to each artifact.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Which two statements are true about practices used with Scrum?
options: Teams may add practices that fit within Scrum and help them create value.
Anything not named in the Scrum Guide is forbidden.
Scrum intentionally leaves many tactics and techniques to the people doing the work.
Only practices approved by the Scrum Master may be used.
explanation: Scrum defines the framework, not every tactic. Teams can use complementary practices as long as they do not undermine Scrum.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Why is the Daily Scrum held at the same time and place each working day?
options: To make it easier for managers to attend.
To reduce complexity and unnecessary coordination overhead.
Because the Product Owner must approve attendance.
To make status reports easier to archive.
explanation: A consistent time and place reduces complexity and helps the Developers focus on inspecting progress and adapting their plan.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A Scrum Master notices a recurring dependency on one external specialist. What is the most useful long-term direction?
options: Keep the dependency hidden so velocity stays stable.
Help the organization and teams reduce the dependency and strengthen the skills needed to deliver value.
Create a permanent approval queue for the specialist.
Make the specialist the Product Owner.
explanation: A Scrum Master should help improve the system around the team, including recurring organizational impediments and dependencies that hurt effective delivery.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Which artifact has the Product Goal as its commitment?
options: Product Backlog
Sprint Backlog
Increment
Definition of Done
explanation: The Product Goal is the commitment for the Product Backlog.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: True or False: The Product Owner can be a committee as long as one person attends Sprint Planning.
options: True
False
explanation: False. The Product Owner is one person, not a committee, even though many people may influence decisions.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: True or False: Scrum requires a special Sprint 0 before the first real Sprint begins.
options: True
False
explanation: False. Sprint 0 is not a Scrum event. Teams begin learning and creating value through regular Sprints.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Which statement best describes self-management in Scrum?
options: The Scrum Master assigns work but Developers may change the order.
The team decides internally who does what, when, and how.
The Product Owner decides who works on each Product Backlog item.
Managers are removed from the organization.
explanation: A self-managing Scrum Team decides internally who does what, when, and how.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Two Scrum Teams on the same product create work that cannot be integrated without a separate integration team. What should concern the Scrum Master most?
options: The product may not have a usable integrated Increment each Sprint.
The Product Owner may have too few meetings.
The teams may have different velocities.
The integration team may need a longer Daily Scrum.
explanation: When teams work on the same product, their combined work needs to create an integrated, usable Increment that meets the shared Definition of Done.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: No manager is assigning tasks inside the team. In Scrum, what should self-management look like instead?
options: The team decides internally who does what, when, and how.
The Scrum Master assigns work but not technical details.
The Product Owner decides who performs each task.
Management decides how work is divided inside the Sprint.
explanation: A self-managing Scrum Team decides internally who does what, when, and how.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Who participates in Sprint Planning?
options: Only the Product Owner and Scrum Master.
The entire Scrum Team.
Only the Developers.
Only people selected by the Scrum Master.
explanation: Sprint Planning is collaborative work for the entire Scrum Team.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Which two problems can come from an unclear Definition of Done?
options: People may have different ideas about whether work is actually complete.
The Product Backlog automatically becomes invalid.
Inspection becomes less reliable because the quality state is unclear.
The Product Owner loses accountability for value.
explanation: The Definition of Done creates a shared understanding of completion. If it is unclear, transparency drops and inspection becomes less trustworthy.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Which event starts the Sprint?
options: Daily Scrum
Sprint Planning
Sprint Review
Sprint Retrospective
explanation: Sprint Planning initiates the Sprint by laying out why the Sprint is valuable, what can be done, and how the chosen work will get done.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Sprint Planning starts with the Product Owner describing a useful outcome for the Sprint. How does the Sprint Goal get established?
options: The Scrum Team together during Sprint Planning.
The Product Owner alone before the event.
The Scrum Master after the event.
The Developers at the Daily Scrum.
explanation: The Scrum Team collaborates to create the Sprint Goal during Sprint Planning.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: At the end of the Sprint, the Scrum Team meets with key stakeholders. What are they there to accomplish?
options: Inspect the Sprint's outcome and collaborate on what to do next.
Approve or reject the Increment.
Rate individual team members.
Finalize every detail of the next Sprint.
explanation: Sprint Review is a working session to inspect the outcome and determine future adaptations.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Which three ideas form the basis of empiricism in Scrum?
options: Transparency.
Inspection.
Adaptation.
Utilization.
Prediction.
explanation: Scrum is founded on transparency, inspection, and adaptation.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Which statement about quality during a Sprint is correct?
options: Quality may be lowered if the Sprint is behind.
Quality does not decrease during the Sprint.
The Product Owner decides when quality can be traded for scope.
Quality is only inspected at Sprint Review.
explanation: One of the rules of the Sprint is that quality does not decrease.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: A Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done at Sprint end. What happens to it?
options: It may be presented as Done if most of the work is complete.
It cannot be considered part of the Increment and returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.
The Scrum Master signs an exception.
It automatically rolls into the next Sprint Backlog.
explanation: Work that does not meet the Definition of Done is not part of the Increment. It remains work to be considered through the Product Backlog.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: Which two actions fit the Scrum Master's service to the organization?
options: Leading and coaching the adoption of Scrum.
Approving every team's Definition of Done.
Helping remove barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.
Acting as the line manager for all Scrum Masters.
explanation: Scrum Masters help the organization understand Scrum and work to remove barriers that make collaboration and empirical delivery harder.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives

prompt: When might canceling a Sprint make sense?
options: When the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.
Whenever one selected item will not be finished.
When velocity is lower than last Sprint.
When a stakeholder asks for a new feature.
explanation: A Sprint may be canceled if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.
source: Shared clean-room Scrum question used in both PSPO I and PSM I practice banks

prompt: Why are shorter Sprints often useful when uncertainty is high?
options: They eliminate the need for Sprint Reviews.
They create more frequent opportunities to inspect results and adapt.
They allow the Scrum Master to assign work more often.
They guarantee higher velocity.
explanation: Shorter Sprints can shorten learning cycles and reduce the amount of risk carried before inspection and adaptation.
source: Original clean-room PSM I-style practice question based on the Scrum Guide and public Scrum.org learning objectives
